preamble: Fronting of a velar stop all the way to a palatalized dental [tʲ] is a rare outcome of velar palatalization; most languages stop at [c] or continue to [tʃ]. It is a defining innovation of the Southern New England Algonquian languages, where Proto-Eastern Algonquian *k became *ty /tʲ/ before PEA *ē and *əw and some reflexes of Proto-Algonquian *i. Massachusett (Wampanoag) thus has wetu /wiːtʲəw/ 'house' where Abenakian and Unami languages keep the velar (wigwam, weekuwôm).

examples.note: The velar became palatalized /tʲ/ (spelled ⟨ty⟩ in the modern orthography) before the weakened vowel; the Abenakian/Unami cognate wigwam, weekuwôm retains k. Palatalization is shared by all Southern New England Algonquian languages, but Quiripi has /tʃ/ rather than /tʲ/.
Contrast sonksquaw /sãkəskʷaː/ 'female chief', where k stays before a consonant.
Palatalization before a schwa that continues an earlier *ī; /k/ is often restored by analogy before /aː/ and /əw/.

sources: Oxford, W. (2023). Consonant inventories from Proto-Algonquian to the daughter languages. https://home.cc.umanitoba.ca/~oxfordwr/algling/consonantchanges.html
